title: Functions and Their Representations
summary: Students learn what a function is, how to identify its domain and range, and how to read functions from tables, graphs, and formulas. They practice interpreting each representation and translating between them.
objectives: Define a function and distinguish it from a relation
State the domain and range of a function from a given representation
Interpret a function presented as a table of values
Read key features of a function from its graph
Translate a function between a formula, a table, and a graph
prerequisites: Students should be comfortable with basic arithmetic, plotting points on a coordinate plane, and understanding variables in simple expressions.
why: Functions describe how one quantity changes with another, which is the basis of everything from calculating speed (distance vs. time) to predicting population growth. Recognising the rule behind a set of data helps you make informed decisions in everyday situations.

In many careers—engineering, economics, computer science—information is given in different forms. Being able to move smoothly between tables, graphs, and formulas lets you analyze data, spot trends, and solve real‑world problems efficiently.

sections.heading: What Is a Function?
sections.body:
A function is a rule that takes a number (or any kind of input) and gives back exactly one number as the result.  
Think of a vending machine: you press a button labelled “A”, and the machine always drops out the same snack.  
Here the button you press is the **input** (we call it $x$) and the snack that appears is the **output** (we write it as $f(x)$).  
The important part is that for each button there is only one snack – you never get two different snacks from the same button.

> **Definition:** A *function* is a relationship between two sets such that every element $x$ in the first set (the *domain*) is paired with exactly one element $f(x)$ in the second set (the *range*).

Why do we care that each input has only one output?  
When we model real‑world situations, we want our predictions to be reliable.  
If the same starting condition could lead to two different results, we could not use the rule to make clear calculations or to draw a single graph.

### The vertical line test

One convenient way to check whether a picture on a coordinate grid represents a function is the **vertical line test**.  
Imagine drawing a straight line that goes up and down (parallel to the $y$‑axis) anywhere on the graph.  

- If that vertical line ever touches the picture at **more than one point**, then at that $x$‑value the picture gives two different $y$‑values.  
  That means the picture is **not** a function, because one input would have two outputs.  
- If every possible vertical line meets the picture at **zero or one point**, the picture passes the test and does represent a function.

Visually, a simple parabola $y = x^{2}$ passes the test, while a circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ fails because a vertical line through $x=0$ meets the circle at two points ($y=1$ and $y=-1$).

$$\text{Vertical line test: } \forall\,\text{vertical line } L,\; |L\cap\text{graph}| \le 1$$

> **Note:** The test works because the $x$‑coordinate is the input. A vertical line keeps $x$ fixed and looks at all possible $y$ values. If more than one $y$ appears, the rule is not a function.

### Everyday comparison

Consider a school timetable.  
Each period (the input) has exactly one subject assigned (the output).  
If period 3 sometimes has Math and sometimes English, the timetable would be confusing and could not be used to plan your day.  
A well‑written timetable, like a function, tells you unambiguously what you will study in each period.

### Building the idea step by step

1. **Input ($x$)** – the value you start with.  
2. **Rule** – the instruction that tells you how to turn the input into an output.  
3. **Output ($f(x)$)** – the single result you obtain after applying the rule.  

If any step tries to give you two different outputs for the same input, the whole construction stops being a function.

> **Common mistake:** Thinking that “a set of points” automatically makes a function.  
> Only when each $x$‑value appears once (or not at all) does the set of points describe a function.

### Why the definition matters

- **Predictability:** Knowing a rule is a function lets you compute $f(5)$, $f(7)$, etc., without guessing.  
- **Graphing:** Functions have graphs that pass the vertical line test, making them easy to draw and interpret.  
- **Algebraic work:** Many algebraic techniques (like solving $f(x)=0$) rely on the fact that each $x$ gives one $f(x)$.

> **Remember:** A function is a one‑to‑one mapping from inputs to outputs *in the sense of “one input → one output”*, not necessarily “one output → one input”. Different inputs may share the same output (e.g., $f(x)=x^{2}$ gives $f(2)=f(-2)=4$), and that is perfectly fine.

sections.heading: Domain and Range Basics
sections.body:
When we talk about a **function**, we are really describing a rule that takes an input, does something with it, and then gives an output.  
The *input* values are called the **domain** of the function, and the *output* values are called the **range**.  

> **Definition:** The **domain** of a function is the set of all possible inputs that the rule is allowed to accept.  
> **Definition:** The **range** of a function is the set of all possible outputs that the rule can produce from those inputs.  

Why do we care about domain and range?  
Knowing the domain tells us where the function makes sense – for example, we cannot divide by zero, so any rule that involves a denominator cannot accept the value that makes the denominator zero.  
Knowing the range tells us what values we can actually get out of the function, which is useful when we need to check whether a particular answer is possible.

### Reading domain and range from a list of ordered pairs  

A function can be written as a **set of ordered pairs**. Each ordered pair looks like $(x, y)$, where $x$ is the input and $y$ is the output that the function assigns to that $x$.  

To find the domain, we simply collect every first component $x$ from the pairs.  
To find the range, we collect every second component $y$ from the pairs.  

Think of the ordered pairs as a menu: the first item tells you *what you can order* (the domain), and the second item tells you *what you will receive* (the range).  

> **In daily life:** Imagine a vending machine that only accepts coins of 1 €, 2 €, and 5 €. The set of accepted coins is the domain. The drinks it can dispense – say, water, soda, and juice – form the range.  

Now let us practice this idea with a concrete example.

---

**Example 1 (Easy): Finding domain and range from a list**  

Given the set of ordered pairs  
\[
\{(2,5),\;(3,7),\;(4,9)\},
\]  
state the domain and the range.

1. **List the first components.**  
   Write down every $x$‑value that appears in the pairs.  
   $$\text{Domain} = \{2,\;3,\;4\}$$  

2. **List the second components.**  
   Write down every $y$‑value that appears in the pairs.  
   $$\text{Range} = \{5,\;7,\;9\}$$  

3. **Check that each $x$ appears only once.**  
   Because a function cannot assign two different outputs to the same input, we verify that the $x$‑values are all distinct (they are).  

**Answer:** The domain is $\{2,3,4\}$ and the range is $\{5,7,9\}$.  

---

### Small steps to avoid common pitfalls  

When you first start, it is easy to mix up the order of the numbers in each pair. Remember that the *first* number is always the input, and the *second* number is the output.

> **Common mistake:** Treating $(5,2)$ as meaning “output 5, input 2”. The correct reading is “input 5, output 2”.

Another frequent error is to think that the domain must be a continuous interval (like all numbers between 1 and 10). With a table of ordered pairs, the domain can be any collection of separate numbers.

> **Remember:** The domain is exactly the set of $x$‑values that appear; it does not have to be “nice” or follow a pattern.

### Why domain and range matter for later topics  

Later we will draw graphs of functions, write formulas, and solve equations. In each of those contexts the domain tells us where the graph will exist, and the range tells us how high or low the graph can go. For instance, the function $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ has domain $x\ge 0$ because we cannot take the square root of a negative number (in the real numbers). Its range is also $y\ge 0$ because a square root never gives a negative result.  

Understanding domain and range now, from simple tables, builds the habit of checking these sets before moving on to more abstract representations.

---

**Example 2 (Medium): Checking a set for function status**  

Consider the set $\{(1,4),\;(2,5),\;(1,6)\}$.  
Is this a function? If it is, give its domain and range.

1. **Look for repeated inputs.**  
   The input $1$ appears in two pairs: $(1,4)$ and $(1,6)$.  

2. **Apply the definition of a function.**  
   A function cannot assign two different outputs to the same input, so the set fails the test.  

3. **State the conclusion.**  
   Because the rule is not a function, we do not list a domain or range.  

**Answer:** The set is **not** a function because the input $1$ has two different outputs (4 and 6).  

---

### Summarising the key ideas  

> **Note:**  
> - The **domain** = all first numbers in the ordered pairs.  
> - The **range** = all second numbers in the ordered pairs.  
> - A set of ordered pairs is a **function** only if each first number appears once.

By practising with tables, you develop an intuitive sense of what inputs are allowed and what outputs you can expect. This intuition will help you when you later translate a function into a graph or a formula, where the domain and range may be expressed with inequalities or intervals instead of simple lists.

sections.heading: Functions as Tables
sections.body:
When we look at a table of numbers, we are often seeing a **function** written out in a very concrete way.  
A function is a rule that assigns to each input value (called the **argument**) exactly one output value. In a table the first column lists the inputs, usually written as $x$, and the second column lists the corresponding outputs, written as $f(x)$ or $y$.  

> **Definition:** A function is a set of ordered pairs $(x,\,f(x))$ such that no two different pairs have the same first component $x$.

Why is this useful?  Tables let us see directly which inputs are allowed and what each input produces.  This makes it easy to find the **domain** (all allowed inputs) and the **range** (all outputs that actually appear).  

> **Note:** The domain is the set of all $x$‑values that appear in the left column; the range is the set of all $y$‑values that appear in the right column.

Think of a vending machine: each button (the input) gives you exactly one snack (the output).  A table for the machine would list each button number and the snack it dispenses.  If a button is missing from the list, you know you cannot press it – that button is not in the domain.  If a snack never appears in the list, the machine never gives it out – that snack is not in the range.

---

### Reading a table step‑by‑step  

1. **Identify the columns.**  The left column is usually the independent variable $x$ (the input).  The right column is the dependent variable $f(x)$ (the output).  
2. **List the domain.**  Write down every distinct $x$ value that appears.  
3. **List the range.**  Write down every distinct $f(x)$ value that appears.  
4. **Look for a pattern.**  Ask yourself how $f(x)$ changes when $x$ changes.  Is it adding a constant, multiplying, squaring, etc.?  This pattern can often be expressed as a simple formula.

---

**Example 2 (Easy): Linear pattern in a table**  

The table shows  

| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
|---|---|
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 6 |
| 4 | 8 |

*Question:* Identify the function rule that relates $x$ to $f(x)$.

1. List the ordered pairs: $(1,2),\;(2,4),\;(3,6),\;(4,8)$.  
2. Observe how $f(x)$ changes: each time $x$ increases by $1$, $f(x)$ increases by $2$.  
3. Guess a linear rule $f(x)=mx+b$.  Use one pair to solve for $m$ and $b$.  
   $$2 = m\cdot1 + b$$  
   $$4 = m\cdot2 + b$$  
   Subtract the first equation from the second: $2 = m$, so $m=2$.  
   Substitute back: $2 = 2\cdot1 + b \;\Rightarrow\; b = 0$.  

**Answer:** The function is $f(x)=2x$.  Its domain is $\{1,2,3,4\}$ and its range is $\{2,4,6,8\}$.

---

Now that we have practiced a simple linear case, let us try a table where the pattern is not immediately obvious.

**Example 3 (Medium): Symmetric pattern and finding domain & range**  

The table shows  

| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
|---|---|
| -2 | 4 |
| -1 | 1 |
| 0  | 0 |
| 1  | 1 |
| 2  | 4 |

*Question:* Determine the domain, the range, and describe the pattern you see.

1. **Domain:** Write all $x$ values that appear.  
   $$\text{Domain} = \{-2,\,-1,\,0,\,1,\,2\}$$  
2. **Range:** Write all distinct $f(x)$ values.  
   $$\text{Range} = \{0,\,1,\,4\}$$  
3. **Pattern:** Look at how $f(x)$ depends on $x$.  Notice that $f(-x)=f(x)$, so the table is symmetric about $x=0$.  The numbers $0,1,4$ are squares of $0,1,2$.  This suggests the rule  
   $$f(x)=x^{2}.$$  
   Check each pair: $(-2)^{2}=4$, $(-1)^{2}=1$, $0^{2}=0$, $1^{2}=1$, $2^{2}=4$.  All match.

**Answer:** Domain $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$, range $\{0,1,4\}$, and the function rule is $f(x)=x^{2}$.

---

### Why tables are a good first step  

Tables give us a **discrete** picture of a function.  Before we draw a smooth curve or write a complicated algebraic expression, we can verify that our proposed rule actually produces the listed values.  This prevents errors later when we move to graphs or formulas.

> **In daily life:** A school timetable is a table that matches each period (input) with a subject (output).  Knowing the domain (the periods that exist) and the range (the subjects taught) helps you plan your day.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming that any two columns automatically form a function.  If a single $x$ value appears with two different $f(x)$ values, the relation is **not** a function.  Always check that each input occurs only once.

---

### Quick checklist for interpreting any table  

- ☐ Are there two columns, one for inputs ($x$) and one for outputs ($f(x)$)?  
- ☐ Does each $x$ appear only once? (If not, it is not a function.)  
- ☐ List the domain: all $x$ values.  
- ☐ List the range: all $f(x)$ values.  
- ☐ Look for a simple arithmetic or algebraic pattern; test it with at least two pairs.  

By mastering these steps, you can move confidently from a simple list of numbers to a full understanding of the underlying function, ready to translate the same information into graphs or formulas later in the lesson.

sections.heading: Functions as Graphs
sections.body:
When we draw a function on a pair of axes, the picture tells us a lot about how the function behaves.  
A **graph** is simply a set of points $(x,y)$ that satisfy the rule of the function.  
Each point tells us that when the input (the *x‑value*) is $x$, the output (the *y‑value*) is $y$.

> **Definition:** *Domain* – the collection of all $x$‑values that appear on the graph.  
> **Definition:** *Range* – the collection of all $y$‑values that appear on the graph.

---

### 1. Locating points on a graph  

To read a graph, pick a vertical line (parallel to the $y$‑axis) at the $x$‑value you are interested in.  
Where that line meets the curve, read the height – that is the $y$‑value.  

*Why it works:* The vertical line fixes the input $x$; the point of intersection shows the corresponding output $y$.

*Everyday comparison:* Imagine a ladder leaning against a wall. If you stand at a certain distance from the wall (the $x$‑position), the height of the ladder at that spot tells you how high you are (the $y$‑position).  

---

### 2. The vertical line test  

A picture can represent many different relationships, but only one that passes the **vertical line test** can be a function.

> **Note:** Draw any vertical line. If it touches the graph **exactly once** (or not at all), the picture is a function. If a vertical line hits the graph twice or more, the picture does **not** represent a function.

*Why it matters:* A function must give **one** output for each input. More than one intersection would mean one $x$ has two different $y$ values, which violates the definition of a function.

*Example of failure:* The graph of a circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ fails the test because a vertical line at $x=0.5$ meets the circle at two points.

---

### 3. Finding domain and range from the picture  

**Domain:** Look left‑to‑right along the $x$‑axis and note the smallest and largest $x$ where the graph exists.  
- If the graph continues forever to the left, the domain extends to $-\infty$.  
- If there is a gap, the domain is split into separate intervals.

**Range:** Look bottom‑to‑top along the $y$‑axis and note the smallest and largest $y$ values that appear.  

*Why it is useful:* Knowing the domain tells us which inputs we are allowed to use; the range tells us what outputs we can expect.

---

### Worked examples  

#### **Example 4 (Medium): Straight line through two points**  

A graph shows a straight line passing through $(0,3)$ and $(2,7)$. Find the function rule and state its domain and range.

1. **Find the slope** – the change in $y$ divided by the change in $x$.  
   $$m=\frac{7-3}{2-0}=2$$  

2. **Write the equation in point‑slope form** using the point $(0,3)$.  
   $$y-3 = 2(x-0)$$  

3. **Simplify to slope‑intercept form** $y=mx+b$.  
   $$y = 2x + 3$$  

4. **Determine domain and range** from the picture of a straight line that extends without end in both directions.  
   - Domain: all real numbers, $(-\infty,\infty)$.  
   - Range: all real numbers, $(-\infty,\infty)$.

**Answer:** The function is $f(x)=2x+3$ with domain $(-\infty,\infty)$ and range $(-\infty,\infty)$.  

> **Remember:** A straight line that is not vertical always passes the vertical line test, so it is a function.

---

#### **Example 5 (Hard): Parabola with given vertex and x‑intercepts**  

A parabola opens upward with vertex at $(-1,-2)$ and crosses the $x$‑axis at $x=1$ and $x=3$. State the domain, range, and write a possible quadratic formula.

1. **Use the vertex form** $y = a(x-h)^2 + k$, where $(h,k)$ is the vertex.  
   $$y = a\,(x+1)^2 - 2$$  

2. **Plug one x‑intercept** (where $y=0$) to find $a$. Use $x=1$:  
   $$0 = a\,(1+1)^2 - 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\cdot 4 = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a = \frac12$$  

3. **Write the full quadratic formula** with $a=\frac12$:  
   $$y = \frac12\,(x+1)^2 - 2$$  

4. **Check the second intercept** $x=3$ to confirm:  
   $$y = \frac12\,(3+1)^2 - 2 = \frac12\cdot16 - 2 = 8 - 2 = 6,$$  
   which is not zero, so we made an error.  
   Instead, use the fact that the roots are $x=1$ and $x=3$, so the factored form is  
   $$y = a(x-1)(x-3).$$  
   Expand: $y = a(x^2-4x+3)$.  

5. **Find $a$ using the vertex** $(-1,-2)$. Substitute $x=-1$, $y=-2$:  
   $$-2 = a((-1)^2 -4(-1) +3) = a(1+4+3)= a\cdot8 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a = -\frac14.$$  

6. **Write the final quadratic formula:**  
   $$y = -\frac14\,(x-1)(x-3) = -\frac14\,(x^2-4x+3).$$  

7. **Domain and range from the picture:**  
   - The parabola exists for every $x$, so domain $(-\infty,\infty)$.  
   - It opens upward, so the lowest point is the vertex $y=-2$. Hence range $[-2,\infty)$.  

**Answer:** A possible function is $f(x)= -\dfrac14(x-1)(x-3)$, domain $(-\infty,\infty)$, range $[-2,\infty)$.  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting that the vertex gives the *minimum* $y$ for an upward‑opening parabola; using the wrong sign for $a$ leads to a downward opening curve.

---

### 4. Quick checklist when you look at any graph  

1. **Vertical line test** – does any vertical line intersect more than once?  
2. **Locate a few points** – read coordinates by dropping a vertical line (for $x$) and a horizontal line (for $y$).  
3. **Identify extremes** – highest/lowest points give range limits; leftmost/rightmost points give domain limits.  
4. **Notice shape** – straight line → linear function; U‑shape → quadratic; repeated waves → periodic, etc.

> **In daily life:** When you look at a speed‑time graph while driving, the vertical line test guarantees that at each moment (each $t$) there is only one speed shown. Reading the graph tells you how fast you were going at any instant, and the highest point tells you your maximum speed (range).

By practicing these steps, you will become comfortable turning a picture into the algebraic description of a function, and vice‑versa.

sections.heading: Functions as Formulas
sections.body:
When we write a function as a formula, we are giving a rule that tells us exactly how to turn an input number $x$ into an output number $f(x)$.  
The formula is like a tiny machine: you feed it a value, the machine follows the arithmetic steps written in the formula, and it spits out the result.  

> **Definition:** A *formula* for a function is an algebraic expression that uses the variable $x$ (the input) and standard operations such as addition $+$, subtraction $-$, multiplication $\times$, division $\div$, and exponentiation $^{}$ to produce the output $f(x)$.  

Why is this useful?  Because a single line of symbols can describe infinitely many input‑output pairs.  Instead of listing a long table, we can compute any value we need, check whether a particular $x$ is allowed, and see how the function behaves overall.

### Reading a formula

1. **Identify the variable.**  
   The symbol that changes, usually $x$, is the *input* (also called the *argument*).  

2. **Follow the order of operations.**  
   Parentheses first, then exponents, then multiplication/division, and finally addition/subtraction (PEMDAS).  

3. **Write the output as $f(x)$.**  
   Whatever the expression evaluates to is the *output*.

For example, in the formula  

$$
f(x)=3x-2,
$$  

the rule says: multiply the input by $3$, then subtract $2$.

### Computing values

To find $f(0)$ we replace every $x$ by $0$:

$$
f(0)=3\cdot 0-2=-2.
$$  

To find $f(4)$ we replace $x$ by $4$:

$$
f(4)=3\cdot 4-2=12-2=10.
$$  

These substitutions are the core of evaluating a formula.

> **In daily life:** Think of a recipe that tells you “use 3 cups of flour for each kilogram of fruit, then subtract 2 teaspoons of sugar.”  If you know the fruit weight (the input), the recipe (the formula) tells you exactly how much sugar to add (the output).

### Domain and range from a formula

The *domain* is the set of all $x$ values we are allowed to plug into the formula without breaking any mathematical rule.  
The *range* is the set of all possible outputs $f(x)$ that result from those allowed inputs.

Two common sources of restrictions:

* **Division by zero** – an expression like $\frac{1}{x-2}$ is undefined when the denominator $x-2$ equals $0$.  
* **Even roots of negative numbers** – $\sqrt{x}$ requires $x\ge 0$ (in the real number system).

When a restriction appears, we simply *exclude* the offending $x$ from the domain.

### Worked examples

**Example 6 (Easy):** *Evaluating a linear formula and listing domain and range*  

For the function $f(x)=3x-2$, compute $f(0)$, $f(4)$ and list the domain and range.

1. **Substitute $x=0$.**  
   $$f(0)=3\cdot 0-2=-2.$$  

2. **Substitute $x=4$.**  
   $$f(4)=3\cdot 4-2=12-2=10.$$  

3. **Determine the domain.**  
   The formula uses only multiplication and subtraction, which are defined for every real number.  
   $$\text{Domain}=(-\infty,\infty).$$  

4. **Determine the range.**  
   A linear function with non‑zero slope takes every real value as $x$ runs over the whole line.  
   $$\text{Range}=(-\infty,\infty).$$  

**Answer:** $f(0)=-2$, $f(4)=10$; the domain and range are both all real numbers.

> **Note:** Linear formulas never create division‑by‑zero or square‑root problems, so their domain is automatically all real numbers.

**Example 7 (Medium):** *Finding domain and describing range for a rational formula*  

For $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}$, identify the domain and describe the range qualitatively.

1. **Look for forbidden operations.**  
   The denominator $x-2$ cannot be zero because division by zero is undefined.  

2. **Solve $x-2=0$ for the excluded $x$.**  
   $$x-2=0\;\Longrightarrow\;x=2.$$  

3. **Write the domain, excluding $x=2$.**  
   $$\text{Domain}=(-\infty,2)\cup(2,\infty).$$  

4. **Think about the output values.**  
   As $x$ approaches $2$ from the left, $g(x)$ becomes a large negative number; from the right, it becomes a large positive number.  
   As $x$ goes to $\pm\infty$, $g(x)$ approaches $0$ but never reaches it.  

5. **Describe the range qualitatively.**  
   All real numbers except $0$ can appear as outputs.  
   $$\text{Range}=(-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty).$$  

**Answer:** The domain is all real numbers except $2$; the range is all real numbers except $0$.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to exclude the value that makes the denominator zero. Always set the denominator ≠ 0 and solve for $x$.

### Extracting domain restrictions systematically

1. **Write down every denominator** and set each ≠ 0.  
2. **Write down every even root** (square root, fourth root, etc.) and require the radicand ≥ 0.  
3. **Write down any logarithm** $\log_b(\text{argument})$ and require the argument > 0.  
4. **Combine all conditions** using “and” (intersection) to obtain the final domain.

### Quick checklist when you see a new formula

- Replace $x$ with the given number to compute $f(x)$.  
- Scan for division, even roots, and logarithms to find domain limits.  
- Remember that the range may need a separate analysis (graph, algebraic solving, or logical reasoning).  

> **Remember:** The formula is a compact description of a function; reading it carefully tells you both how to compute values and which inputs are allowed.

sections.heading: Translating Between Representations
sections.body:
When we talk about “translating between representations” we mean that the same function can be shown in three different ways:  

* a **table** that lists a few input–output pairs,  
* a **graph** that draws those pairs on a coordinate plane, and  
* a **formula** (or rule) that tells us how to compute the output for any allowed input.

Being able to move from one picture to another is useful because each representation highlights something different. A table is quick for checking a few numbers, a graph shows overall shape and trends, and a formula lets us compute any value without drawing. Think of a recipe: the list of ingredients (table), the picture of the finished dish (graph), and the step‑by‑step instructions (formula). All describe the same meal, and a good cook can read any of them and still know what to make.

---

> **Note:** *Domain* is the set of all inputs we are allowed to use, and *range* is the set of all outputs that actually appear. When we change representation we must keep the same domain and range; otherwise we are describing a different function.

### Step 1 – From a rule to a table  

First we start with a simple rule and write down a few values.

**Example 8 (Hard): Create a table, sketch the graph, and confirm domain and range for \(f(x)=2x+1\).**  

We are asked to list the outputs for the inputs \(-2,-1,0,1,2\).

1. **Choose the input values** (the given \(x\)-values).  
2. **Apply the rule** to each input: compute \(f(x)=2x+1\).  

   $$f(-2)=2(-2)+1=-4+1=-3$$  
   $$f(-1)=2(-1)+1=-2+1=-1$$  
   $$f(0)=2(0)+1=0+1=1$$  
   $$f(1)=2(1)+1=2+1=3$$  
   $$f(2)=2(2)+1=4+1=5$$  

3. **Write the table**  

| $x$ | $f(x)$ |
|-----|--------|
| -2  | -3     |
| -1  | -1     |
| 0   | 1      |
| 1   | 3      |
| 2   | 5      |

**Answer:** The table above lists the first five points of the function.

Now we **draw the graph** by plotting each ordered pair \((x,f(x))\) on the coordinate plane and connecting them with a straight line (because the rule is linear). The line continues indefinitely in both directions, so the **domain** is all real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) and the **range** is also all real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\).  

> **Remember:** When the rule is a linear expression like \(2x+1\), the graph is a straight line extending without end, giving an infinite domain and range.

### Step 2 – From a table to a formula  

Next we start with a table and try to guess the rule that could have produced it.

**Example 9 (Very Hard): Infer the formula from the table \(\{(0,1),(1,4),(2,9),(3,16)\}\), write it, and draw its graph.**  

1. **Observe the pattern** in the outputs: \(1,4,9,16\). These are perfect squares: \(1^2,2^2,3^2,4^2\).  
2. **Relate each output to its input**. When \(x=0\) we get \(1= (0+1)^2\); when \(x=1\) we get \(4=(1+1)^2\); when \(x=2\) we get \(9=(2+1)^2\); when \(x=3\) we get \(16=(3+1)^2\). The pattern suggests  

   $$f(x) = (x+1)^2$$  

3. **Check the formula** by plugging each \(x\) from the table.  

   $$f(0) = (0+1)^2 = 1$$  
   $$f(1) = (1+1)^2 = 4$$  
   $$f(2) = (2+1)^2 = 9$$  
   $$f(3) = (3+1)^2 = 16$$  

   All match, so the inferred rule is correct.

4. **Sketch the graph** of \(y=(x+1)^2\). This is a parabola opening upward, shifted left by 1 unit (the vertex is at \((-1,0)\)). Plot the four points from the table and draw a smooth curve through them.

**Answer:** The formula is \(f(x) = (x+1)^2\); its graph is a parabola with vertex \((-1,0)\). The domain is all real numbers, and the range is \([0,\infty)\) because a square is never negative.

> **In daily life:** Converting a price‑list (table) into a pricing rule (formula) lets a shop owner quickly compute the cost of any quantity without writing down every possible total.

### Step 3 – Keeping domain and range consistent  

Whenever we move between representations we must ask two questions:

* Are we using the same set of allowed inputs?  
* Do the outputs we obtain cover exactly the same set as before?

If we forget, we might unintentionally restrict the function. For instance, if we only list the five points from Example 8 in a table, the **apparent range** looks like \(\{-3,-1,1,3,5\}\). But the true range of the rule \(f(x)=2x+1\) is all real numbers. The graph reminds us that the function continues beyond the listed points.

> **Common mistake:** Assuming the range of a function is just the numbers that appear in a small table. Always refer back to the original rule or the full graph to determine the true range.

### Summary of the translation process  

1. **Rule → Table:** Choose a convenient set of input values, substitute them into the rule, and record the outputs.  
2. **Table → Graph:** Plot each ordered pair \((x,f(x))\) on the coordinate plane; connect points according to the nature of the rule (line for linear, curve for quadratic, etc.).  
3. **Graph → Rule (or Table → Rule):** Look for patterns—constant differences suggest linear rules, constant second differences suggest quadratic rules, etc. Test a guessed formula on the listed points.  
4. **Check domain and range** at each step to ensure they stay the same.

By practicing these conversions, you develop flexibility: you can read a graph and immediately write down a formula, or glance at a table and picture the shape of the curve. This skill is essential for solving problems where the information is given in a form different from the one you need.

practice.q: Given the table below, write a formula for the function and state its domain. | $x$ | $f(x)$ | |-----|--------| | -1  | 1      | | 0   | 2      | | 1   | 3      |
practice.a:
Look at how $f(x)$ changes when $x$ increases by 1: the output increases by 1. This suggests a linear rule $f(x)=x+2$. Check:
- For $x=-1$: $-1+2=1$ ✓
- For $x=0$: $0+2=2$ ✓
- For $x=1$: $1+2=3$ ✓
Domain is all listed $x$ values, i.e. $\{-1,0,1\}$ (or, if we assume the rule holds for all real $x$, the domain is $\mathbb{R}$).
---

practice.q: Sketch the graph of $g(x)= -x+4$ for $x=0,1,2,3,4$ and state whether it passes the vertical line test.
practice.a:
Compute points:
- $x=0$: $g(0)=4$ → (0,4)
- $x=1$: $g(1)=3$ → (1,3)
- $x=2$: $g(2)=2$ → (2,2)
- $x=3$: $g(3)=1$ → (3,1)
- $x=4$: $g(4)=0$ → (4,0)
Plot these points and draw a straight line through them. Any vertical line cuts the line at most once, so it **passes** the vertical line test; therefore it is a function.
---

practice.q: The piece‑wise function $h(x)$ is defined by $$h(x)=\begin{cases} 2x+1 & \text{if } x<2\\[4pt] 5   & \text{if } x\ge 2 \end{cases}$$ Create a table of values for $x=0,1,2,3$ and then write the set of ordered pairs that represent the function.
Determine the domain and range of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}$.
practice.a:
The denominator cannot be zero, so $x-2\neq0\;\Rightarrow\;x\neq2$.
**Domain:** all real numbers except $2$, i.e. $(-\infty,2)\cup(2,\infty)$.
For any allowed $x$, the output $f(x)$ can be any real number except $0$ (because $1/(x-2)$ is never zero).
**Range:** $(-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)$.
---

practice.q: A function $p$ is given by the formula $p(x)=\sqrt{4-x^2}$. 1. Find its domain and range. 2. Write a table with $x$ values $-2,-1,0,1,2$ and the corresponding $p(x)$. 3. Sketch the graph and explain why it fails the vertical line test if we tried to define $y=\pm\sqrt{4-x^2}$ as a single relation.
practice.a:
1. Inside the square root must be non‑negative: $4-x^2\ge0\;\Rightarrow\;x^2\le4\;\Rightarrow\;-2\le x\le2$.
So **domain** is $[-2,2]$.
The largest value of $p(x)$ occurs at $x=0$: $p(0)=\sqrt{4}=2$. The smallest is $0$ (when $x=\pm2$).
Hence **range** is $[0,2]$.
2. Evaluate:
- $x=-2$: $p(-2)=\sqrt{4-4}=0$
- $x=-1$: $p(-1)=\sqrt{4-1}= \sqrt{3}$
- $x=0$: $p(0)=\sqrt{4}=2$
- $x=1$: $p(1)=\sqrt{3}$
- $x=2$: $p(2)=0$
Table:
| $x$ | $p(x)$ |
|-----|--------|
| -2  | 0      |
| -1  | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| 0   | 2      |
| 1   | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| 2   | 0      |
3. Plot the points; they lie on the upper half of a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin (equation $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$, $y\ge0$).
If we tried to use $y=\pm\sqrt{4-x^{2}}$, the graph would include both the upper and lower semicircles. A vertical line at, say, $x=0$ would intersect this relation at two points $(0,2)$ and $(0,-2)$, violating the vertical line test. Therefore $y=\pm\sqrt{4-x^{2}}$ is **not** a function, while $p(x)=\sqrt{4-x^{2}}$ (the upper half only) is a function.
---

practice.q: Consider the function defined by the rule $q(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}$ for all $x\neq2$. 1. Simplify the expression and state the new formula. 2. Determine the domain and range of $q$. 3. Explain why the graph of $q$ has a “hole” at $x=2$ and how this affects the function’s definition.
practice.a:
1. Factor numerator: $x^{2}-4=(x-2)(x+2)$. For $x\neq2$ we can cancel the common factor:
$$q(x)=\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=x+2,\qquad x\neq2.$$
So the simplified formula is $q(x)=x+2$, but we must remember $x=2$ is excluded.
2. **Domain:** all real numbers except $2$, i.e. $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{2\}$.
Using the simplified rule $x+2$, the outputs would be all real numbers, but we must check the missing input $x=2$. At $x=2$, the original expression is undefined, so the output $q(2)=4$ is **not** attained. Therefore the **range** is $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{4\}$.
3. The graph of $y=x+2$ is a straight line. Because the original definition forbids $x=2$, the point $(2,4)$ is omitted; this creates a “hole” (a removable discontinuity). The function is still well‑defined for every allowed $x$, but it is **not** the same as the full line $y=x+2$; the hole indicates that the rule $q(x)=x+2$ does not apply at $x=2$. If we wanted a function without a hole, we would need to redefine it by setting $q(2)=4$, which would give a new function equal to $x+2$ on all real numbers.

recap: A function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to each input, described by its domain and range. Functions can be shown as tables, graphs, or formulas, each giving a different view of the same relationship. Understanding domain prevents illegal inputs, while range tells what outputs are possible. Translating between representations helps solve problems more flexibly.

key_terms.meaning: A rule that gives one output for each input.
The set of all allowed input values.
The set of all possible output values.
A pair written as (x, y) showing an input and its output.
A picture of all ordered pairs that satisfy the rule.
An algebraic expression that computes the output from the input.
A list of input‑output pairs arranged in rows.
A way to check if a curve represents a function by ensuring each vertical line meets it at most once.

quiz.q: What must be true for a rule to be a function?
options: Each input has at most one output
Each output has at most one input
The graph is a straight line
quiz.why: A function assigns exactly one output to each input.

quiz.q: Which of the following could NOT be in the domain of f(x)=1/(x-3)?
quiz.why: x=3 makes the denominator zero, which is not allowed.

quiz.q: In a table of a function, what does the left column represent?
quiz.why: The left column lists the input values, i.e., the domain.

quiz.q: What does the vertical line test check?
options: If the graph is a parabola
If each x‑value appears only once
quiz.why: A vertical line intersecting the graph more than once means one input has multiple outputs.

quiz.q: Which representation lets you compute f(7) without drawing or looking up a table?
quiz.why: A formula provides a direct calculation for any allowed input.

quiz.q: If a function’s range is {2,4,6}, which statement is true?
options: The function outputs only even numbers
The graph is a straight line
quiz.why: All possible outputs are even numbers, matching the given range.
